title: Narada's sorrow and the sound of the Veda
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: a sage knows every mantra by heart and still asks to be taken across
carry: shruti is kept by sound, opened by meaning
tomorrow: peace for whom? one chant names the sky, the water, the trees.

cards: In the Chandogya Upanishad, Narada, the wandering sage, comes to the teacher Sanatkumara and says: teach me, sir. Tell me what you know first, says Sanatkumara.
So Narada lists it: the Rig Veda, the Yajur, the Sama, the Atharva, the old histories and stories, grammar, the rites for the ancestors, numbers, the stars, and on and on.
Then he says the line the whole story turns on: sir, I know only the mantras; I don't know the self. I've heard that whoever knows the self crosses beyond sorrow. I am in sorrow.
Take me across. Sanatkumara's first answer is blunt: all that you've learned is only name. And he starts leading him, step by step, toward the self.

teach.b: So is the sound of a chant enough, or must it be understood? Inside Hinduism, both answers have serious defenders. First, the side of sound.

The Vedas are called shruti, what was heard: tradition holds the ancient seers heard them, and for many centuries they were kept by mouth and ear, teachers having students repeat every word and every pitch in set patterns so nothing would drift.
Many hold that a mantra's sound does its work even before the meaning arrives. Its best case: without that care, there'd be no words left to understand. Now the side of meaning.

teach.h: YASKA: A POST CARRYING A LOAD.
teach.b: Yaska, an early explainer of hard Vedic words, says someone who learns the Veda by heart without knowing its meaning is like a post, a wooden pillar carrying a load it knows nothing about.
And Narada's story says what the meaning is for: the words are kept to lead somewhere, to knowing the self, the atman, which many teachers read as one with Brahman, the reality in everything.
Narada could recite it all and was still in sorrow. So here's the teaching.
In Hinduism, the sacred sound is treasured, and it's a doorway, not the room. Here's where it meets now. Nani tells Priya: just say it, beta; the meaning comes when it comes.
Priya wants the assembly to know every word. Nani's way is how the chant reached Priya at all. Priya's way is Narada's request.
Narada needed both: a lifetime of sound, and then a teacher to open it.

how: Vedic reciters learn texts by ear from a teacher, word by word and pitch by pitch; others study the meanings through commentaries and teachers. Some families chant first and learn meanings later; some learn both together.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: a well-known verse and peace chants, read one word at a time
a book of rules for building fire altars correctly
prayers chanted only in silence, never aloud

games.q: sound and sense — tap the pairs.
p: knew every mantra, not the self
said all that learning is only name
what was heard: kept by mouth and ear
carries a load it doesn't know

s: Narada came to Sanatkumara sure that knowing the mantras was enough
he said: I know only the mantras, not the self, and I am in sorrow.
the Vedas were kept for centuries by mouth and ear
shruti, what was heard: every word and pitch repeated in set patterns.
reciters who keep the exact sound think meaning is worthless
that's a caricature; their care is why the words survive to be understood.

games.q: Nani says 'just chant it; meaning can come later.' Priya disagrees. before she argues, what's the strongest case for Nani's side?
o: the words have no meaning at all; only the sound counts.
the sound, kept exactly by mouth and ear, is why the words still exist.
Sanskrit is too hard for anyone to understand now.
games.why: the reciters' best case: without their care for sound, there'd be nothing to read. and Yaska's best case: a chant never understood is carried, not received.

practice: Say shanti out loud three times as pure sound, letting the n hum and the ending breathe out. Then say it three more times, holding its meaning, peace, in mind as you do.
Sit afterward and notice, without judging, whether anything felt different.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: shruti, what was heard, kept by sound and opened by meaning.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sthanu, a post or pillar; Yaska's picture of a reciter who doesn't know the meaning.

carryVoice: Your line: shruti is kept by sound, opened by meaning. Say the words; then ask what they're for. Day fifteen-oh-eight, done.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.1–3 (Narada comes to Sanatkumara, lists all he has studied, says he knows the mantras but not the self (mantravid evasmi natmavit) and is in sorrow; Sanatkumara: all this is only name)
Nirukta 1.18 (the reciter who does not understand, likened to a post bearing a load; the one who knows the meaning)
